title: Council Post: 2 Ways AI Is Reshaping The Future Of Digital Marketing
text:
Krishan Arora is CEO & Founder at Arora Project, a globally recognized leader in raising investor capital & scaling high-growth ventures.
In the ever-evolving world of digital marketing, there have been a few pivotal moments over the past three decades that have defined the entire industry. For example, the internet boom of the early 2000s led to the formation of social media platforms, which led to the multibillion-dollar digital advertising industry as we know it today.
One of the major shifts in the last decade was going from desktop-first to mobile-first, and we can all see how the adoption of mobile-first has changed everything we do today from ordering rides via Uber to ordering groceries via Instacart all on our mobile phones.
A second tectonic shift is taking place right now, yet many do not realize the true impact this radical shift will have on every single one of us on planet Earth. The era of artificial intelligence is upon us, and it is going to radically change almost everything we do in the digital marketing world.
As a marketing expert for the past 15 years, and having spent tens of millions of dollars on social media advertising campaigns (with a focus on delivering a high ROI for our clients), I can already see two very clear areas where AI will completely revolutionize digital marketing:
• The advancement of predictive analytics.
• AI-based content creation.
The Advancement Of Predictive Analytics
Before AI entered the conversation, using analytics to predict customer behavior involved several touch points from humans. We had to isolate which metrics were important to us, extract large sets of data, use tools to sift through it and then find meaningful patterns to test to see whether we could predict customer behavior. Some tools were helpful in this space before AI was present, but the process was still largely manual and cumbersome with limited efficiency.
Now, predictive analytics powered by AI are revolutionizing how we forecast customer behavior, make key decisions and identify important trends within e-commerce. Using the raw computing power of tools like Google's Gemini or OpenAI's ChatGPT, we can input massive datasets, and the AI engines will sift through them and recommend in seconds key metrics and hypotheses to test. This ability to analyze and digest large sets of digital marketing data gives us the ability to make key decisions much faster, and this speed increases with every optimization made.
AI-Based Content Creation
By far, content creation is the most impacted area of digital marketing in this new era of AI. First came AI-generated text—email copy, ad copy and landing page copy—which can be created within a matter of seconds. By entering the correct prompts, you can get copy that is witty, smart and relevant to a specific region of the world.
Then came AI-generated images through programs such as Midjourney and DALL-E that take prompts and create images right in front of your eyes. Over the past year, these image generators have gotten much better, and many other image generators have been created on top of these AI engines.
Then came the final straw that broke the metaphorical camel's back: OpenAI released Sora, its prompt-to-video generator that generates incredible video clips from prompts.
Even though this AI-powered content creation world is still in its nascent stage, the AI platforms are evolving and getting better literally week after week. Soon the entire content creation engine within digital marketing could be powered not by specialists who create copy or images or video, but by prompt specialists who engage with AI tools to create content in real time.
Looking Ahead: Adapt Or Get Left Behind
The era of AI radically shifting every system we use in digital marketing is upon us. Even tools such as the Google search engine, something we never thought would be innovated upon, are now being threatened by AI tools such as ChatGPT. Users around the world are leaning into AI tools and large language models to help make their workflows much more productive.
My advice for marketing team leaders and professionals is to adopt these technologies to boost your and your team's efficiency. By embedding these content creation and predictive analytics engines within your workflows, you can be 300% to 500% more effective in terms of your output, essentially doing the jobs of three to five people.
The ability to do more high-quality work in less time is the main attractiveness of these AI tools. It's not a matter of whether or not you should adopt these technologies—it's really (more dauntingly) a matter of either adopting these tools and staying competitive, or not staying relevant in the marketplace anymore. AI is here to stay, and the future is very bright in the world of AI-based digital marketing.

title: Council Post: Four Key GovTech Trends For 2024
text:
Tom Amburgey is the CEO of Euna Solutions, a leading provider of purpose-built, cloud-based solutions for the public sector.
In 2024, the landscape of governmental technology, or GovTech, is undergoing transformative changes, reshaping how state and local government operations are conducted. These advancements are not only enhancing the efficiency and accessibility of public services but also addressing the ongoing challenges of security, privacy and operational management.
This article highlights four key GovTech trends for 2024, exploring how cloud computing, cybersecurity, artificial intelligence (AI) and edge computing are setting new benchmarks for the public sector.
Greater Migration To The Cloud
One of the most significant shifts in GovTech is the migration to the cloud. Governments worldwide are embracing the potential of cloud technologies to streamline operations, enhance collaboration and improve service accessibility. This transition isn't just about adopting new technologies—it represents a fundamental shift toward digitizing manual practices and functions and signals a move toward a more efficient and interconnected public sector.
However, the path to cloud adoption is fraught with challenges. The inherent risks associated with software malfunctions, project delays and other potential failures require state and local governments to be cautious. Ensuring proper staffing, understanding cloud software and implementing standards and best practices are crucial steps toward minimizing risks and accommodating public concerns effectively.
Security Remains A Top Concern
Cybersecurity has ascended to a critical level of importance, especially as cyber threats evolve with increasing sophistication. As governments worldwide push forward with digital transformation initiatives, securing sensitive information against threats is more pressing than ever. This focus on security is integral to a broader initiative to enhance data protection and privacy safeguards.
The challenge for governments lies in adopting innovative technologies and ensuring that these technologies are fortified against potential security breaches. Such breaches pose risks to personal data and national security alike. This increased focus on security signifies a profound recognition of the ramifications associated with digital progress and a steadfast dedication to preserving citizen trust and safety in an increasingly digital world. Consequently, bolstering cybersecurity measures has become a crucial element of GovTech's strategy, emphasizing its fundamental role in the architecture of contemporary governance and the provision of public services.
Artificial Intelligence Arrives
The advent of AI in state and local governments signifies a crucial shift toward more efficient and streamlined public service delivery. With the potential to transform how services are delivered, AI-driven automation can reduce the administrative load, enhance process efficiency and deliver services more effectively to the public.
This movement is further bolstered by President Biden's AI Executive Order, which highlights a national commitment to ensuring that AI deployment is regulated, ethically aligned and used responsibly across all levels of government. The order is particularly relevant to automating intricate government functions, including budgeting, grants management and procurement processes, in which AI can significantly impact efficiency and transparency.
However, as AI technology is integrated into the fabric of governmental operations, there's a pressing need to vigilantly monitor its implementation to prevent its misuse, guarantee its alignment with ethical standards and ensure that AI's deployment brings about the intended benefits of enhanced service delivery while upholding the principles of equity and fairness. The balance between leveraging AI's capabilities and safeguarding ethical values is essential for realizing the full potential of AI in transforming government services.
Edge Computing Gains
Edge computing is also gaining momentum, promising to simplify further governmental processes such as registrations, licensing and permitting. As state governments issue mandates for edge computing, local governments are expected to follow suit, adopting standards that support cloud infrastructure and foster collaboration. Despite the potential of edge computing, challenges related to privacy and security, particularly in the face of sophisticated phishing attacks and social engineering campaigns, remain a concern. Nevertheless, ongoing improvements in digital processes signal significant advancements in edge computing capabilities, contributing to the digital transformation of the public sector.
In conclusion, the GovTech landscape in 2024 is poised for significant advancements made possible by technological innovation. These trends reflect a broader movement toward digitalization, aiming to enhance operational efficiency, security and service delivery in the public sector. As governments navigate the challenges and opportunities presented by these technologies, the focus will remain on ensuring ethical deployment, safeguarding privacy and minimizing risks. The journey toward a digitally transformed government is complex and ongoing, but the progress made in 2024 is expected to lay a strong foundation for the future of public sector operations.

title: Council Post: How AI Will Bolster Machine Identity Management
text:
Gregory Webb is the CEO of AppViewX, a cybersecurity and IT infrastructure automation platform enabling digital transformation.
Two of today's fastest-growing technology developments—artificial intelligence (AI) and machine identity management (MIM)—are on a collision course when it comes to enterprise security, for both good and bad. While AI and machine learning (ML) are both transformative and disruptive technologies, there is currently a lot of uncertainty about how these technologies will define best practices in identity management. What we do know today is that cyberattackers, as well as cyber defenders, will have powerful new capabilities that will continue to evolve.
When it comes to security threats, AI can equip adversaries with potent new capabilities for launching more effective strikes faster than ever. These threats range from advanced automated scripts to exploiting known cryptographic vulnerabilities and weaknesses and even using identity deep fakes that specifically target machine identities.
However, AI is not just a tool for adversaries. With the surging number of machine identities associated with devices, workloads, applications, virtual machines and cloud services, an acute and often overlooked lack of visibility and control over the trustworthiness of these assets is leading to critical security blind spots.
This is primarily because machine identities rely on digital certificates issued by both public and private trust certificate authorities (CAs) to ensure the security and authenticity of the connections between devices, protect sensitive data and maintain the integrity of networked systems.
Since these vast numbers of certificates have expiration dates that require continual renewals to maintain trust and encryption capabilities, AI can serve as a powerful ally to implement a proactive, identity-first security strategy to defend against evolving threats. For example, AI can be used to automate the discovery of new machine identities faster and more comprehensively. Together with ML capabilities, AI can help facilitate the auto-provisioning of new and the renewal of expiring digital certificates that support machine identities and digital trust in line with established security policies.
The role of AI in MIM extends beyond just mitigating risks. AI can be harnessed to enhance machine identity security to champion zero-trust initiatives in the following ways.
• Automated Identity Discovery And Management: AI can continuously monitor and discover new entities within a network, automatically assigning and managing digital certificates based on predefined security policies. This not only ensures that every entity is recognized and secured with a trusted identity but also reduces the administrative burden on IT staff.
• Anomaly Detection And Response: By learning normal user and machine behavior patterns, AI, together with ML, can detect identity anomalies associated with critical vulnerabilities or cryptographic weaknesses that could be used for unauthorized access or to compromise identities.
• Identity Analytics: AI-driven analytics provide deep insights into an organization’s identity fabric as well as usage and patterns, enabling security teams to make informed decisions for defining and modifying identity and access controls and security policies.
• Advanced Threat Intelligence: AI can analyze vast amounts of data to detect machine identity vulnerabilities and potential threats, provide predictive insights and enable security teams to preemptively address security issues.
• Regulation And Compliance: With regulatory requirements becoming more stringent, AI can help ensure a state of continuous compliance by automating the monitoring and reporting of identity lifecycle management processes, thereby reducing the risk of non-compliance violations.
As critical security instruments that make up the identity infrastructure of every modern enterprise, digital certificates are always under attack. Meanwhile, their lifespans will continuously get shorter (Google has proposed reducing TLS validity to 90 days), and new threats are coming with post-quantum cryptography. In light of these increasing challenges, AI can play an important role in an organization's certificate lifecycle management strategy. Here are some best practices to consider when implementing AI as part of an MIM security program.
• Customizable AI Algorithms: Given the unique nature of different organizational environments, AI algorithms in MIM should be customizable. Organizations should be able to tailor AI models to their specific network architectures, types of digital assets and security policies. This customization ensures that AI solutions are not just generic but are fine-tuned to the specific needs of the organization.
• AI-Driven Identity Lifecycle Management: Implement AI to manage the entire lifecycle of machine identities, from creation and renewal to decommissioning. This includes automated provisioning, rotation and revocation of credentials and certificates. This approach ensures that outdated or compromised identities are promptly removed or updated, maintaining a robust security posture.
• Real-Time Analytics And Reporting: Utilize AI for real-time analytics and reporting to provide immediate insights into identity security status. This includes monitoring the issuance, usage and expiration of digital certificates and identifying irregularities in real time, enabling swift response to potential vulnerabilities and security incidents.
The integration of AI and ML capabilities into MIM will enable a new era of identity-first security and automated zero-trust frameworks to counter new threats and maintain compliance. The explosive growth in machine identities, which is only accelerating, will make AI and ML even more indispensable in establishing trust and securing an organization’s digital assets. There is still a lot to learn about the power of AI and ML, and we are really just scratching the surface as to their capabilities for keeping organizations protected from new threats and attacks.

title: What Entrepreneurs Need To Know To Leverage AI In Creating Faster Startups
text:
Like the Internet and perhaps mobile before it, Ai offers many potential benefits for startup businesses, including increased efficiency, cost savings, new kinds of customer service, and growth opportunities. Ai tools today are software that use algorithms to carry out requests, tasks and can be useful for automation. Their potential applications for entrepreneurs include automating business processes and analyzing information for better planning and decision making. So, what do we do with this powerful new tool, or as some would see it, in the entrepreneurial process of creating new startups?
Babson, a very entrepreneurial college, has a point of view based on an article they published in their magazine in the summer of 2023. The article, The Age of AI: Seven Things Entrepreneurs Need to Know, provides several insights which we will examine on behalf of entrepreneurs who are considering the use of Ai in their existing or new startups. Ai is a fascinating new tool or even platform that can conjure up a prototype image of a can of sparkling water, perhaps craft that perfect email or even create a new company logo. But at what price? Will we create mediocre or passable work at the cost of creative design? Will Ai ultimately cost people their jobs or will it be a compliment to perform mundane tasks and routines?
We don’t know yet but this technology is too powerful to ignore, so at a minimum, you need to know what you don’t know about Ai. Here are some insights:
You don’t need to code to write code. One of the early uses of Ai is to create prototypes of things based on just text requests. Write a better email based on these prompts, create a line of code that makes a simple change to a shopping cart checkout, design a website that will sell leather handbags and so on. For perhaps the first time, non-programmers will be able to create ‘things’ that were, in the past, left to software architects and coders. While there will be downsides perhaps, the other side of this coin is rapid prototyping and trial and error at lightning speed.
Knowledge acquisition speed will triple. It used to be that if you wanted to know something you did not know; you went to the universities of Google and YouTube where you could spend 20 minutes or two hours finding or viewing information and then try and make a determination of how helpful that information might be. Now, in less than 10 seconds, you can get, based on prompts or questions, a dissertation of exactly how something works and perhaps even a suggestion of a better version. You could do something fairly mundane like have an Ai tool write a proposed travel policy. Or you could ask it to examine your competitors social media marketing and look for insights. Either way, the speed of data or information gathering will be amazing.
Prototyping reality. As an entrepreneur, especially with a new startup, you are trying to showcase your vision for the new company in as many ways as possible. Well, with Ai, you can utilize the tool to create a small plan, a business model, then prototype a new website, an image of the new product, a social media ad, a spokesperson demo video and a financial forecast. Fast. Like perhaps over a weekend if you are super-efficient with an Ai tool. It will all look fairly real but not be perfect. But if you want rapid feedback, from either customers or investors, it will help you present your ’dream’ as if it were already real.
Regardless of your point of view on Ai, it is here. As Ai tools and platforms grow, entrepreneurs will have to strike a balance and navigate ethical considerations. While Ai can enhance decision-making, prototyping and automate processes, it will still need both technology and human expertise. Ethical situations will arise, as will legal issues regarding copyrights and so on. But at a minimum, entrepreneurs should investigate and ‘play’ with these new sets of tools as some of them will be gamechangers.

title: Council Post: Leveraging Generative AI And LLMs In The Industrial IoT Realm
text:
Srikar Kasarla is Senior Vice President of Technology & R&D at Schneider Electric.
The world of technology is witnessing the unfolding of a transformative era with the arrival of generative AI and large language models (LLMs). This innovative technology is shaping up to offer solutions for tackling complex challenges and unlocking new possibilities of creativity and innovation. By having the ability to generate content—be it text, visual, sound, data or code—generative AI has the potential to revolutionize industries far and wide.
In the last decade, the Internet of Things (IoT) has completely changed many industries. It's been a catalyst, sparking a revolution that has reimagined the limits of what we thought was achievable. IoT has turned the traditional workings of numerous sectors inside out. As sensors and smart devices started to pop up everywhere, embedding themselves into the very fabric of industries, IoT has firmly established itself as the foundation upon which modern industry stands.
Combining the power of generative AI and IoT opens up a realm of new possibilities and opportunities. Generative AI offers a wide range of capabilities that can enhance IoT applications and use cases in several ways. These capabilities include:
• Synthetic data and data augmentation.
• Anomaly detection.
• Data anonymization.
• Natural language interface.
• Automation.
Let's take a closer look at each of these capabilities.
Synthetic Data And Data Augmentation
IoT devices generate lots of data, which is crucial for training machine learning models. But, collecting real-world IoT applications data can be both costly and challenging, often due to complex IoT deployments, security and privacy concerns.
Generative AI presents a solution by creating synthetic datasets that closely mirror real-world conditions. This approach enables the efficient training and testing of machine learning models for various IoT scenarios. By generating data that simulates real device telemetry, generative models can enhance the diversity and quality of datasets, addressing issues of data scarcity, imbalance or incompleteness. This augmented data supports the development of more accurate machine learning models for applications such as energy forecasting and occupancy planning, ultimately improving the functionality and efficiency of IoT systems.
Synthetic data, which is data generated by AI models to mimic real-world data, also helps in predictive maintenance. Generative AI, by utilizing historical data, failure patterns and real-time information, can generate synthetic data to simulate various operational conditions and failure scenarios, which can help forecast potential equipment malfunctions and recommend proactive measures to avoid them. This helps significantly reduce downtime and maintenance costs in Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) environments.
Anomaly Detection
Anomalies in IoT data, such as sudden spikes or irregular patterns, can indicate potential equipment failures, security breaches or abnormal behavior that require immediate attention.
Generative AI offers a solution to detect anomalies within IoT environments by learning normal operational patterns from vast amounts of device data and identifying deviations that could indicate potential issues or security threats. Unlike traditional threshold-based systems, generative AI models can understand complex, multidimensional device data, enabling them to detect subtle anomalies that might otherwise go unnoticed.
This capability is particularly valuable in scenarios where IoT devices monitor critical infrastructure, manufacturing processes or environmental conditions, where early detection of anomalies can prevent equipment failure, production downtime or environmental hazards.
Data Anonymization
In the IoT ecosystem, data sharing is essential for analytics use cases, research purposes and collaboration with third parties like system integrators. However, IoT data often contains personal or confidential information, which makes sharing the data complex and challenging.
Generative AI models offer a solution through data anonymization. Data anonymization, as the name suggests, allows anonymizing the data while preserving the statistical properties of the data. These anonymized datasets can be utilized for analysis, development and testing, aligning with data protection regulations without risking data privacy.
The flexibility and power of generative AI in anonymizing data makes it very valuable for organizations aiming to leverage IoT data for analytics, machine learning or sharing with third parties.
Natural Language Interface
The utilization of industrial IoT data by end users often involves complex graphs, intricate data tables and complex user interfaces. Using and understanding these graphs and user interfaces demands a certain level of technical proficiency and familiarity with the IoT application's structure.
Generative AI presents an opportunity to simplify this process. Generative AI enables the usage of natural language for consuming complex IoT data, which helps address the complexities associated with navigating data graphs, tables and user interfaces. Using natural language, users can ask questions, issue commands or request information from IoT devices using conversational language, making interactions more intuitive and user-friendly.
Automation
Operations in IoT environments include several activities, like device configurations, issuing commands to devices, creating and executing workflows and more. These activities are very critical, and most of them need human involvement.
Generative AI can automate routine tasks and optimize operations in IoT environments. By interpreting natural language commands and understanding context, generative models can autonomously control IoT devices, adjust device configuration and execute workflows without explicit human intervention. For example, generative models can schedule recurring tasks, manage device configurations or optimize resource allocation based on user preferences and environmental conditions.
Harnessing AI
By harnessing the power of generative AI, organizations can build more innovative, intuitive, intelligent and user-centric IoT solutions. These solutions can improve operational efficiency, productivity and customer satisfaction and drive transformative change across diverse domains.
Despite the promising opportunities offered by generative AI in IoT, there are few challenges that need to be addressed to realize its full potential. Some of the key challenges include the complexity and cost of generative model development, integrating these generative AI models into existing IoT environments, ensuring regulatory compliance and many others. Overcoming these obstacles involves collaboration among technology teams, regulatory bodies and industries to leverage generative AI's potential to enhance IoT environments responsibly.

title: Council Post: The Paradox Of Progress: Embracing AI Advancements While Navigating Challenges
text:
Inc. 5000 entrepreneur, martech and AI thought leader, co-founder of Ntooitive Digital and Nloop.AI.
In the ever-evolving landscape of technological advancements, each leap forward brings with it a mixture of excitement and apprehension. This is not new. Electricity, microwaves, radio, the internet, telephones—all of these now-commonplace technologies were once feared.
In the 19th century, the Luddites engaged in acts of sabotage by breaking cost-saving textile machinery, concerned this new technology would replace workers and lower wages. Does this sound familiar?
Even Socrates begrudged the written word because he thought it would weaken the capacity for memory and threaten the oral tradition. (Though we know this because, luckily for us, his student Plato wrote down these arguments.)
Today, amid the AI revolution, many people are echoing similar sentiments. But looking to the past, history reveals that despite initial hesitation, transformative technologies do become part of our lives and quickly.
As we navigate the early stages of this AI era, it’s crucial to recognize and address both the opportunities and challenges that these powerful tools present. AI is not a passing fad—it is an indelible part of our future.
Is AI taking over jobs?
Since its public release in November 2022, OpenAI’s chatbot, ChatGPT, has been the subject of wide discussion, especially around replacing human workers.
But this concern may be a bit misguided. When Microsoft launched spell check in the 1990s, for example, it wasn’t about teaching people how to have perfect spelling. It was offloading a non-creative task, in which no human could ever achieve 100% accuracy to computers. Today, tools like Grammarly's corrective grammar tool likely won’t improve your grammar, but it can improve the readability of your writing by identifying errors and making suggestions.
As stated in Asana’s State of AI at Work, employees reported that 29% of their tasks could be replaced by AI. Automation has already taken over a lot of data analysis and admin work, but this is not necessarily a bad thing. In fact, one of the more significant benefits of AI is its ability to automate mundane tasks, freeing up time for other endeavors.
In other words, a robot might not replace you, but you could be replaced by another person who is proficient in AI if you aren't. Tools such as Grammarly and Zapier can speed up a workflow, but they still need to be operated by a human. Those who learn AI and are adept at AI tools will stand out in the workforce against those who are not.
Marketers, for instance, can embrace AI for its ability to augment their abilities rather than threaten their roles. By leveraging AI for tasks like data analysis and automation, marketers can focus on strategic planning and creative work. I’ve never met a marketer who wishes for more time with spreadsheets and less time connecting with customers and creating a brand story.
Building Trust In AI
As with all new technology, trust must be established. Developing trust in the public for AI requires efforts centered on transparency and ethical practices.
Trust in AI also requires human oversight. The human-in-the-loop model, for example, combines the computing power of AI with the decision-making of humans. Working in a loop of continuous interactions between humans and machines, the result is something neither could do alone—with improved judgment.
There’s a legitimate concern that AI-generated content may lack the authenticity and human touch the consumer relies on. Tasks that involve creativity, abstract concepts or thinking outside the box, such as forming a compelling and unique marketing campaign, are often better performed by humans. Tasks involving massive amounts of data, such as real-time optimization and personalization of content delivery, would be impossible for a human to replicate.
Informing a client or consumer about the use of AI is also essential for establishing principles of responsible use. When AI is used, whether it be for copy or images, share that information with the client. Be transparent about when (and how) AI is being used. This is key to building trust in a developing industry and disruptive technology.
Conclusion
As we navigate the nascent era of AI, it’s important to recognize that AI is not inherently good or bad—it’s how we choose to use it determines its effect. When used ethically, with the guiding principle of transparency, we can have the best of both worlds, where machine-human collaboration works together to drive innovation.

title: This Startup Wants To Be OpenAI Of Stem Cell Therapy, Targets $250B Market
text:
Five scientists walked into a lab late last year and decided to establish a startup combining their wide-ranging expertise, practical experience and breakthrough innovations. The goal of their startup, Somite.ai, is to improve the lives of millions of people by leveraging AI to produce human tissue for cell therapies. The market for the therapies for the diseases they aim to address is estimated at $250 billion.
Somite.ai is a potent mix of state-of-the art stem cell biology, medicine, genetics, engineering, statistics, computer science, and machine learning. The co-founders are Olivier Pourquie, Professor of Genetics, Harvard Medical School and of Pathology, Brigham and Women’s Hospital; Allon Klein, Associate Professor of Systems Biology, Harvard Medical School; Cliff Tabin, Professor and Chair of Genetics, Harvard Medical School; Jonathan Rosenfeld, Head of the Fundamental Foundation AI group at MIT FutureTech; and Micha Breakstone—his PhD is in Cognitive Science, but he opted for a non-academic career, becoming a successful AI entrepreneur (selling Israeli startup Chorus.ai for $575 million, among other endeavors).
“We're developing life language models,” says Breakstone, “we're literally learning the game of life.” Many established biotech companies and startups today are trying to better understand cell development and establish new paths to cell replacement therapy or CRT. What makes Somite.ai stand out in this crowded market?
In addition to assembling a dream team, Breakstone points to three fundamental differentiators: the focus on somites; using embryo digital twins (a computational model representing the composition and organization of an embryo) to guide and control the discovery, optimization and production variability in CRT; and novel use of AI.
Somites are the embryonic structures that are responsible for producing the musculoskeletal system and related tissues. “No other lab today can produce Somites at our level of efficacy and accuracy,” says Breakstone. In 2015 and 2016, Pourquie published two seminal papers demonstrating how to develop these type of cells in an effective way.
Meanwhile, Klein and other researchers successfully integrated tools from molecular biology, engineering, statistics and computer science, to produce “movies” showing how, in the words of Science, “a single fertilized egg gives rise to the multitude of cell types, tissues, and organs that fit together to make a body.” Klein, who received the James Prize for this breakthrough, says: “This technology is essentially the foundation now for turning developmental biology, which has been an expert-driven science, into a data science.”
The new insights into cell differentiation and tissue development paved the way to today’s cell replacement therapy. “It’s the most sophisticated therapy that has ever been invented,” says Klein. Instead of therapies based on a drug delivered to a cell, now the treatment itself is “a living cell that can sense, respond, form tissues, regenerate.” CRT today, says Klein, represents enormous potential but also enormous complexity.
The key challenge for CRT is to find the step-by-step instruction set that leads to the desired cell types at large scale, with minimal contaminants of unwanted cell types, and with high reproducibility. The two main approaches for achieving this goal are “direct programming” (through a process known as gene editing) and “guided differentiation.”
The gene editing strategy, says Klein, is a “very exciting” vision, promising that “if you can just bring cells right to the end point, they will figure everything else out and they will become physiologically normal.” Somite.ai, however, adheres to the slower and safer guided differentiation approach, convinced that “every single step that the cell goes through in the process of development is important for shaping its final function and identity. And we need to take cells as closely as possible through these steps in order to make sure that we get to the end point.” The environment in which the cell grows “can matter a great deal,” says Klein.
The new, data-rich approach to understanding cell differentiation and tissue development, the creation of embryo digital twins and the accumulation of data generated by many labs have led to a data explosion. For example, data from single-cell RNA sequencing is currently doubling every six months.
This is where AI can make a big difference. “Data by itself is valuable, but we need to know how to use this data systematically. We also need to update the data continuously, to take what we learn in the dish and feed it back into a system which can learn on the fly,” says Klein. Self-supervised machine learning, trained on existing data troves and what’s produced in the lab, coupled with the knowledge contained in thousands of papers published in recent years mined by text-processing domain-specific large language models, facilitate automating and accelerating the discovery and optimization of the step-by-step guide to successful CRT.
Somite.ai announced last week that it has raised $5.3 million in pre-seed funding. The round was led by TechAviv, joined by Next Coast Ventures, Trust Ventures, Texas Venture Partners, Lerer Hippeau and others. The startup has already hired two translational scientists, experienced in the complex process of commercializing FDA-approved treatments. Targeting therapies that have the potential to cure a wide range of diseases that involve the loss or deficiency of cell populations such as muscular dystrophies, obesity and diabetes, Somite.ai plans to bring, within the next two years, its first therapeutic asset to phase-1 clinical trials.
“The future of medicine lies at the intersection of AI and biology,” says Breakstone. Successfully realizing this vision entirely depends on the quality of human intelligence involved, on melding together the best of multiple scientific disciplines, and on the art of seeing around corners.

title: Why Generative AI Will Help Us Build A More Resilient Workforce
text:
We are on the cusp of a genuine breakthrough in improving workforce performance, as AI helps us take quicker, smarter, and more impactful action to build organizational and individual resilience.
I’ve been in the business of helping major, multinational companies build workforce resilience for more than a decade. Now, a once-in-a-generation change is upon us. With generative AI, we will soon surmount one of the biggest obstacles to improving how people work and live: making vast, complex workforce well-being data accessible, understandable, and actionable.
The power of resilient workforces for business growth is undeniable. As AON research shows, organizations that improve well-being increase company performance by up to 55%. In my company, we’ve helped our customers lower turnover, decrease burnout, and save millions of dollars by building the resilience of their workforce.
This work begins with methodologically rigorous data collection on core psychological factors that influence workforce performance. For example, which departments have strong problem-solving skills, or lack a sense of trust? Which division shows emotional signs of stress, such as anger or frustration?
Data collection is non-negotiable. You can’t fix what you can’t see. At the same time, we are more motivated to fix what we can see, especially when we understand why performance and engagement problems are occurring and how to address them.
Getting to that “why” is the hard part. A tremendous amount of complex information comes out of the data collection. Leaders typically do not have the skills or the staff to analyze it, let alone operationalize it. Training up or hiring new staff isn’t affordable for most businesses. In an era of scarce labor, finding the right talent is itself a problem.
If we can’t make sense of the data, we can’t see what’s really happening in our workforces. We end up spending money on the wrong things, attempting to solve problems that might not be the vital issues. We’re feeling our way in the dark.
We turn the lights on with generative AI.
Pair thorough psycho-cognitive data collection with the astounding analytic capacity of generative AI, and we get sophisticated workforce insights faster, more efficiently, and in ordinary language. We will not need Ph.D.-level analyst support to understand what the information’s telling us. We’ll be able to enhance and advance our well-being and resilience data in a snap. With generative AI, we can be the data professionals who truly know what’s going on in our companies.
With this analysis, C-suite leaders and managers alike will also be able to see clearly which actions best foster resilience in their people. The clarity will in turn equip us to take swift, accurate, and effective action.
What’s more, as we build our generative AI tools to speak in natural language, we’ll be able to share our data insights with colleagues and supervisors simply and persuasively. The all-important “why” that drives engagement—from individual employee behavior change for greater resilience to CHRO sign-off on a resilience initiative—will be at our fingertips.
With generative AI tools, business and HR leaders will be able to:
- Be more connected to our businesses. AI will help us identify, with unprecedented speed, which specific business units are struggling with resilience and in which ways. If sales has low confidence, or a shipping unit has high anxiety, we’ll be able to pinpoint those trends precisely.
- Understand how motivational and behavioral factors drive performance. These tools will show how underlying psychosocial factors drive engagement, i.e., how lack of confidence relates to burnout rates, or how poor emotion control can drive low productivity.
- Operationalize our knowledge. Generative AI will help us connect data analysis with action. Which resilience-based interventions are proven to best improve chronic frustration? What’s our most effective path to greater problem-solving skill? Then we’ll be able to deploy those plans.
- Share insights across departments and job roles. No longer will we struggle to convey what we’ve learned to our customers and colleagues. With precise insights delivered in ordinary language, generative AI lets all stakeholders see how key psycho-cognitive factors impact performance and how to most effectively address them. We’ll be able to see the likely upside of taking action, as well as the risk of doing nothing
Generative AI to build resilience in the workforce may well be revolutionary technology. Let’s be clear, though. AI is not the endgame. It is only a tool, and one that needs strong, ethical standards to govern our use of it. But as we develop this tool, as it helps us see and solve problems better and faster, it will accelerate our power to build exceptional workforces, grow our businesses, and know what it takes to help people work and live at their best.

title: Artificial General Intelligence Is Pure Hype
text:
When OpenAI's board momentarily ousted Sam Altman from his post as CEO last November, the media obsession was... intense. Why so much fuss about a corporate drama? The public mania—and perhaps the ousting itself—came in no small part from a widespread belief that the company is well on its way to accomplishing its stated mission, the formidable goal of building artificial general intelligence, software capable of any intellectual task humans can do.
If it came true, AGI would be the whole enchilada. Today’s systems only accomplish narrow, well-defined tasks. For example, predictive AI—aka enterprise machine learning—draws from data to improve large-scale business operations, such as targeting marketing, fraud detection and various kinds of risk management activities. And generative AI creates drafts of writing, code, video and music. In contrast, since AGI would be as generally-capable as humans—across all jobs, including the performance of AI research itself—the implications would be earth-shattering.
But the belief that we’re gaining ground on AGI is misguided. There’s no concrete evidence to demonstrate that technology is progressing toward general human-level capabilities. Reports of the human mind's looming obsolescence have been greatly exaggerated.
This mistaken belief should be tempered by AGI’s immense difficulty. How could we build it? The human species is flummoxed. Even if the human mind could be emulated or equaled by a computer program—even if human abilities are algorithmic—the real difficulty comes in how to program it in the first place. Just because computers are so general-purpose that they hold the potential to do almost anything does not mean they will do everything we envision. And just because computers will soon potentially equal the human brain's sheer computational power quantitatively—in terms of the number of operations per second—that doesn't contribute to the qualitative development needed to stand up to the brain's functions. The power is in the instructions we give the device, not in the device itself.
But journalists, futurists and other purveyors of hype promote this myth with full immunity because it’s unfalsifiable. It may be hard to prove true, but it's impossible to prove false. We could never be certain whether AGI is on its way until its alleged arrival.
Nonetheless, even if we can't disprove the claim that AGI is nigh, we can examine its credibility as much as any other outlandish, unfalsifiable claim. To date, no advancements have provided clear insights as to how to engineer human-level competence that is so general that you could assign the computer any task that you might assign to a person. Speculating on that possibility is no different now, even after the last several decades of impressive innovations, than it was back in 1950, when Alan Turing, the father of computer science, first tried to define how the word "intelligence" might apply to computers.
That’s tough news for the AI industry, which has bet the farm on AGI. And for media darlings who enjoy a special sort of glamor and intrigue—as well as the occasional stock bump—for declaring that AGI is coming soon, including Altman (OpenAI), Bill Gates (Microsoft), Demis Hassabis (Google DeepMind), Jensen Huang (Nvidia), Elon Musk (Tesla) and Mark Zuckerberg (Meta).
Unfortunately, AGI is the last great hope for artificial intelligence. AI is a buzzword looking for meaning. It sounds like it must mean something particular, but it does not consistently identify any specific technology or cohesive idea. While some use "AI'' to simply mean machine learning, it’s generally meant to convey something more. What exactly? There are two main camps. One accepts the vagueness of the word “intelligence” in their conception of AI. The other seizes upon a goal that’s unambiguous yet quixotic: They proclaim that AI is meant to be capable of no less than everything. Why not define it that way, if you believe AGI is around the corner?
Since the day the term was coined, AI has faced this identity crisis. It’s stubbornly nebulous, so proponents continually perform an awkward dance of definitions that I call the AI shuffle. Some say that AI is intelligence demonstrated by a machine, but that’s too vague to constitute a pursuable engineering goal. Some define AI in terms of an advanced capability, but that also falls short—when a computer drives a car or plays chess, it's still only considered a primordial step rather than AI in the full sense of the word. Still others refuse to define it entirely; even some popular books on the topic offer no definition whatsoever. While some fans of the AI brand find its amorphous nature charming, that's a bug, not a feature. If you can't concretely define it, you can't build it.
The best way out of this predicament would be to drop the term AI entirely (outside of philosophy and science fiction) and stick with machine learning, a well-defined, proven technology. But AI has become a powerful brand, riding strong on tremendous momentum. And so, to establish a concrete definition, it must eventually resort to the ultimate, grandiose goal, AGI. Doing so is divisive indeed—many insiders prefer more modest goals for AI as a field. But since those less anthropomorphic goals elude any clear, satisfactory definition, AI's identity consistently reverts back to AGI.
AGI presents such a gargantuan requirement for technology that even just validating its existence would be impractical within the brief, decades-long time ranges that many bet on. For example, developers could benchmark a candidate system’s performance against a set of, say, 1 million tasks, including tens of thousands of complicated email requests you might send to a virtual assistant, various instructions for a warehouse employee you'd just as well issue to a robot and even brief, one-paragraph overviews for how the machine should, in the role of CEO, run a Fortune 500 company to profitability. You'd then have to wait and see how those companies fare over long periods.
Let's call AGI what it is: artificial humans. In this story, the computer essentially comes alive. We must not let impressive developments—including the advent of generative AI—propel wild beliefs about the impending arrival of superintelligence. Instead, pivot from grandiose goals to credible ones. The false promise of creating AGI within mere decades leads to poor planning, incurs great cost, gravely misinforms the public and misguides legislation.

text:

Italy considers tougher penalties for AI-related crimes
The document, whose content is still subject to change, envisages use of such tools in the health sector and in the judiciary, focusing on its impact on job conditions. It also sets the ground for a national AI strategy.
Italy's government is mulling tougher penalties for crimes using Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools including market rigging and money laundering, according to a draft law bill seen by Reuters on Tuesday.
The 25-article draft bill lays down general principles "on research, experimentation, development, adoption and application" of AI in Italy, to cope with "the impact on fundamental rights" and related economic and social risks.
The document, whose content is still subject to change, envisages use of such tools in the health sector and in the judiciary, focusing on its impact on job conditions. It also sets the ground for a national AI strategy.
The draft beefs up penalties for market rigging through AI tools and stipulates that the use of AI for money laundering represents an aggravating element.
It also sets out fines for copyright violations through AI and a jail term of up to three years for those who employ such tools to replace other persons, potentially targeting harmful deepfakes.
Italy currently holds the rotating chair of the Group of Seven (G7) major democracies. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has said AI will be among the key issues of the 2024 presidency which will culminate in a leaders' summit in the middle of June.
AI has also become a crucial issue in the European Union. The bloc is moving closer to adopting the world's first rules on such tools, which will have to comply with specific transparency obligations and EU copyright laws.
In March, Meloni said she was planning to set up an investment fund to promote AI projects with an initial endowment of 1 billion euros ($1.1 billion). The fund could raise a further 2 billion euros from the private sector.
Italy's cabinet is expected to give an initial green light to the bill by the end of April, two government sources said.
The proposal will then be pushed through parliament for any further revisions and final approval before becoming effective.

text:

Meta debuts new generation of AI chip
"This chip's architecture is fundamentally focused on providing the right balance of compute, memory bandwidth, and memory capacity for serving ranking and recommendation models," the company wrote in a blog post.
By Max A. Cherney
SAN FRANCISCO: Meta Platforms unveiled details on Wednesday about the next generation of the company's in-house artificial intelligence accelerator chip.
WHY IT IS IMPORTANT
Reuters reported earlier this year that Meta planned to deploy a new version of a custom data center chip to address the swelling amount of computing power necessary to run AI products in Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp. The chip, referred to internally as "Artemis," will help Meta reduce its reliance on Nvida's AI chips and reduce its energy costs overall.
KEY QUOTE
"This chip's architecture is fundamentally focused on providing the right balance of compute, memory bandwidth, and memory capacity for serving ranking and recommendation models," the company wrote in a blog post.
CONTEXT
The new Meta Training and Inference Accelerator (MTIA) chip is part of a broad custom silicon effort at the company that includes looking at other hardware systems too. Beyond building the chips and hardware, Meta has made significant investments in developing the software necessary to harness the power of its infrastructure in the most efficient way.
The company is also spending billions on buying Nvidia and other AI chips: This year CEO Mark Zuckerberg said the company planned to acquire roughly 350,000 flagship H100 chips from Nvidia. Combined with other suppliers, Meta plans to accumulate the equivalent of 600,000 H100 chips this year, he said.
THE NUMBERS
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co will produce the new chip on its "5nm" process. Meta said it is capable of three times the performance of its first generation processor.
WHAT IS NEXT
The chip has been deployed in the data center and is engaged in serving AI applications. The company said it has several programs underway "aimed at expanding the scope of MTIA, including support of (generative AI) workloads."
